items.title: Knicks Domino Effects: What if Jalen Brunson stayed in Dallas?
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
Domino effects are meant to start relatively small. The first two editions of the series, I feel like, encompassed that. We got really niche with the Mike Brown Kings saga and less niche with Julius Randle’s injury, but both of them required a lot of outside-the-box thinking to see directly what a reversal would’ve caused to the Knicks’ long-term hopes.

This one is anything but niche.

To wrap up this mini-series I’ve had fun with over the dog days of the summer, we’re going to look at possibly the biggest domino effect of them all, one that was scarily realistic and only didn’t occur because of the hubris of a certain front office that later made one of the worst trades in NBA history.

You saw the title. This is a scenario that Jalen Brunson, the birthday boy and the man who has exceeded every expectation and has spearheaded a revival of Knicks basketball so grand that all of us have spent way too much money on championship merch, never puts on the orange and blue.

Following his third season in Dallas, Brunson and his agents at CAA wanted to negotiate a contract extension with the Mavericks’ brass. The number that they decided on was more than reasonable for a player of his current production: four years and $55 million. After all, he was coming off finishing fourth in Sixth Man of the Year voting with plausible upward mobility.

Dallas said no. Fast forward a few months: as Brunson began what turned out to be a breakout campaign, he and his agent approached the Mavs again about the same framework and were again told no.

Brunson kept working and gradually improving to the point where the Mavs themselves approached him about the $55 million deal after the trade deadline, but at that point, he had outgrown that offer as he was barreling towards free agency. Four months later, he landed in New York on a four-year, $104 million pact.

But what if Dallas realized what they had in Brunson at either one of those points, particularly the in-season extension? What if they took a guy that the Knicks had long been looking at off the market? Such a deal would’ve been more than reasonable for their current cap structure as a sixth man or starter next to Luka Doncic, even if the fit was potentially difficult due to both of their defensive shortcomings. Frankly, it was nonsensical for them to be that blind. This was a good player.

December 1, 2021. Jalen Brunson and the Dallas Mavericks announce a four-year, $55 million extension that will begin the following season. Let’s see where the dominoes fall.

Nothing changes from this point forward on any side for the rest of the 2021-22 season. Brunson still balls out and gets on the national radar with his incredible performance in the postseason; the Knicks still miss the playoffs, etc. Instead of the media clowning the Knicks for giving Brunson a nine-figure deal in June, the offseason is spent lauding Nico Harrison and company for their wherewithal to lock down this impact player for cheap.

Of course, this creates a gigantic path of divergence for the Knicks, who were always infatuated with Brunson because of his family connections. I still think Rick Brunson gets hired onto Tom Thibodeau’s staff to replace the outgoing Kenny Payne (who had a truly disastrous tenure at Louisville). The hiring was definitely motivated by his son’s free agency, but he had also served as an assistant under Thibs in Chicago and Minnesota, so it still happens.

The real question, though, is what happens in that offseason. Our first major question revolves around the strategy for the 2022 NBA Draft, particularly with the No. 11 overall pick.

For those who don’t remember, the Knicks selected Ousmane Dieng, traded him to the Thunder in exchange for three first-round picks, traded up to No. 13 in exchange for two picks, selected Jalen Duren, and shipped him to Detroit alongside Kemba Walker in an effective salary dump. The team came out with solid assets and cleared up some cash.

The motivation behind punting a lottery pick? Signing Jalen Brunson. A later trade with Detroit shipped Alec Burks and Nerlens Noel to the Motor City and cleared up just enough space for the Villanova alum and Isaiah Hartenstein in free agency. It’s why I never cared about people saying “the Knicks traded Jalen Duren for nothing” because it’s false. You don’t get Brunson (most likely) without trading Duren, his cap hit, and the salary attached.

But with Brunson off the table and no clear reason to use cap space, the Knicks are dead set on picking in the lottery. You might think it’s as simple as drafting Dieng or Duren, but the Knicks almost certainly made both selections on behalf of the teams they were actively negotiating with. After all, if they wanted them, they wouldn’t trade them.

There were a few plans for this draft leading up to it. After the Knicks were once again denied a chance at lottery luck, they constantly rang the phones to try to trade up for Jaden Ivey. They may get over the line for this. After all, with no Brunson on the way, there are no schematic issues.

It would still be a very difficult trade to make, so I lean toward it not happening. After Ivey, they seemed quite enamored with Wisconsin guard Johnny Davis, but the Wizards took him 10th overall. That’s two major bullets dodged, but who’s on the clock at No. 11?

The available players who had a pre-draft workout in New York were AJ Griffin, Tari Eason, MarJon Beauchamp, and Mark Williams. I would think it would be one of these guys, even if the extremely talented Jalen Williams and Duren were on the board. In typical Leon Rose fashion, he probably does the first two trades of the night, where he trades out and comes back in, ultimately scooping up two conditional firsts from Detroit and Washington while trading four seconds.

With the 13th pick, they select Duke wing AJ Griffin.

With no Brunson and an unsuccessful pursuit of both Davis and Ivey in the draft, the Knicks badly need a point guard. I’d assume they still look to offload salary, particularly with Kemba, to open cap space, but the extent of this is unclear due to the lack of a clear alternative in free agency. There’s restricted free agent Collin Sexton, of course, but the direction that needs to be taken appears to be in the trade market.

Fortunately, there are two lead guards available.

Dejounte Murray is on the block in San Antonio and could be had for a reasonable package. His defensive fortitude makes him a welcome fit for a team that has major defensive questions, and his offense has also proven capable of a leap forward. There’s also that New York native out in Utah who could be of use…

For Murray, the Knicks never seemed that motivated to make that move, even if he would’ve been a decent fit next to Brunson in real life. They were always more focused on adding Donovan Mitchell and figuring it out later. In this timeline, Murray still goes to Atlanta, but it’s a full-court press on bringing Spida home.

With no Brunson, there’s nothing holding them back from adding a small guard into the fray. The fit concerns aren’t there. When Danny Ainge and the Jazz ask for a ridiculous package, it’s eventually negotiated down into something the team can agree on.

In mid-August 2022, Mitchell comes home for a package centered around RJ Barrett and Quentin Grimes, depleting the team’s draft capital to keep further players out of the deal. As much as fans want to play the kids, the Knicks see an opportunity to compete and take it.

Thus, here’s the rotation we have heading into the 2022-23 season:

Donovan Mitchell – Derrick RoseEvan Fournier – Immanuel Quickley

Alec Burks – Cam Reddish/AJ Griffin

Julius Randle – Obi Toppin

Mitchell Robinson – Isaiah Hartenstein

Yes, in this reality, we assume that the Knicks still find a way to get off Noel’s contract but keep Burks as wing depth after trading Barrett and Grimes. Hartenstein was always a target for the front office and still comes to New York.

This lineup, as you might imagine, would’ve been rather erratic. You have some brilliant shotmakers in there, but not enough defenders. Tom Thibodeau’s seat gets hot again; he’s forced to bench some players permanently, and the mini-revival still happens… to an extent.

Quickley gets a chance to start with Spida, Deuce McBride’s emergence happens a year sooner, Randle enjoys his bounce-back season. The foundation of the start of the Brunson era would’ve likely been similar, but the real repercussions come later.

At the deadline, the team needs wing depth, having iced Reddish out of the rotation. With Brunson no longer on the team, I can’t imagine the interest in Josh Hart is any more pronounced. It’s still possible that the trade happens. I’m instead going to involve the Knicks in the multi-team trade with the Warriors and Pistons that got Gary Payton II back to the Bay. The Knicks send a bucket of seconds and Cam Reddish to Detroit for Saddiq Bey.

With Mitchell, the Knicks win 48 games and slide into the fourth seed in the Eastern Conference, where they host a Cavs team that never got the New York native and instead had to continue building around Darius Garland, Sexton, and Evan Mobley. The Knicks still win in five.

In the second round, the Bucks still get slayed by the wrath of Jimmy Butler and the Heat, and although many fans are optimistic about the prospects of facing the No. 8 seed, Butler waxes the Knicks in a six-game defeat.

Heading into the following season, the Knicks are content with what they got, planning to use it as a building year. Burks never being traded means there’s not enough space to sign Donte DiVincenzo, who was also likely going to be someone Brunson pitched signing. There’s no big move to be made here, so we keep going into a shaky start to the 2023-24 season, which leaves them at an inflection point around the New Year.

As you might recall, OG Anunoby was acquired in real life on December 30, 2023, for RJ Barrett, Immanuel Quickley, and a second-round pick. In this reality, Barrett is already gone, but Quickley is becoming a foundational piece after being started out of necessity midway through the prior season. The financials still work if the Knicks add Burks to the trade, but with Barrett not included, the rest of the team’s excess draft capital goes with it.

The Big 3 of Spida-Anunoby-Randle destroy the competition in January 2024 until injuries take out both Randle and Anunoby. Mitchell does his best to imitate 2024 Brunson and gets First-Team All-NBA for his troubles, but it’s certainly an uphill climb. Without DiVincenzo to help with off-ball scoring, the Knicks only win 46 games, dropping them to the play-in tournament. Remember, the No. 2 and No. 7 seeds were just three games apart that year.

The Knicks get revenge on the Heat in the 7-8 game, but have to fare with a road series against Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Bucks in the first round, one that just doesn’t go well. With no Randle to physically match up, Toppin (who I believe doesn’t get traded with the team’s worst depth the prior season) and Precious Achiuwa are overwhelmed in a six-game defeat. The front office blames injuries and doesn’t make any drastic moves… yet.

The Mikal Bridges trade never happens. They had to use a boatload of draft assets to get Anunoby and Mitchell, so the Nets aren’t interested. Anunoby extends, Spida gets his three-year, $150 million extension, and the Knicks seem prepared to run it back in 2024-25.

Now, you might wonder: what about KAT?

The Knicks badly wanted him, but they lacked a guy who Minnesota really valued in DiVincenzo to get it done. Further, the fact that Mitchell took a max extension puts the team eerily close to the second apron, something they avoided with Brunson’s pay cut. There’s a very realistic world that this trade doesn’t happen, but Leon Rose always gets his guy, so they trade Mitchell Robinson and the last bits of draft capital to get it done.

It’s not worth prognosticating who fills the Hart and Bridges gaps in the lineup, but the Knicks are built around Mitchell, Anunoby, and Towns. That Big 3 would get two seasons to work everything out, going into the second apron in 2025-26 before James Dolan would order a restructuring. They had to win. They had no choice.

In the first year, they get bounced in the second round by the Celtics after a 52-win season. The poise of the Brunson-led Knicks was a big part of why they came back from all those deficits, plus the team would be utterly devoid of defensive length without Robinson or Bridges. This also means that the Knicks and Pacers never rekindle their rivalry in either season, which is fun to think about.

In 2025-26, the year we all rejoiced in real life, they had a real chance. They fortified the depth; they hired Mike Brown to replace Thibs; they waltzed into an extremely weak East and grabbed the bull by the horns.

50 wins in the regular season, enough for the No. 3 seed. They survived a seven-game war with Atlanta, took out Philadelphia in six games, and went face-to-face with the Pistons in the ECF. Remember, no Mitchell likely dooms the Cavs to mediocrity and no ECF berth.

It’s hard to say for sure if the Pistons give the Knicks the same fits they did in real life, but let’s look at the facts. The Knicks were still a major question mark defensively and had no answer for Cade Cunningham. Additionally, they lacked the presence of Robinson (even in a backup role) to fluster Duren. In a tense, seven-game series, the Pistons prevailed. It’s over.

Mitchell would not be extended again by the Knicks, as his playoff shortcomings would not be worth the $270 million extension he got in real life. I’d think the front office would side with the Big Bodega in this, and the team would be built around the fleeting prime of Towns from here.

Safe to say, no banners. Sad stuff. But how’s Jalen doing in Dallas?

Brunson’s New Life In Dallas

Dallas did basically nothing that offseason to replace Brunson, leaving them inherently weaker entering the 2022-23 season. They still acquire Christian Wood after retaining Brunson, but they feel pretty stagnant.

The big change in the 2022-23 season is that the Mavericks never traded for Kyrie Irving, as the fit with him, Brunson, and Luka would’ve been quite bizarre. They also wouldn’t feel the need to, as when Doncic goes down with injury right before the deadline, we see glimpses of Knicks Brunson in the emerging Villanova alum.

Dallas was quite bad this season, flaming out in the play-in tournament, but an interesting trickle-down effect from this is that they wouldn’t be able to properly tank to keep their draft pick, so a parting gift from Brunson would give the Knicks a lottery pick in 2023, which they’d use on a guy like Jordan Hawkins. Not a needle mover, so I didn’t feel the need to mention until now.

The reverb would be no Dereck Lively II in Dallas, but the supporting cast from guys like PJ Washington and eventually Daniel Gafford would provide enough for the Mavericks to still go deep in the postseason in 2024, maybe making the NBA Finals but still not coming that close to a title.

At the same time that all appears to be well in Dallas, Nico Harrison is stirring. He doesn’t like the frequent unavailability of Doncic, who still suffers a major hamstring injury on Christmas 2024. In his absence, unlike in real life where Kyrie suffered a multi-week injury as well, the Mavericks experience the joy of 2024 Jalen Brunson, who carries Dallas through January to the point where Harrison has an epiphany.

“What if I fortify my defense and Jalen can give me Luka-esque production?”

Brunson’s explosion dooms Doncic’s tenure, as the controversial trade with the Lakers still occurs. Anthony Davis would now be paired with a head of the snake in Brunson, a match seemingly made in heaven.

Except Davis is still injury-prone. Dallas never has the death spiral they had with Davis and Irving’s season-ending injuries because Brunson would be there trying to play hero ball. He does just enough to win them 45 games to take the No. 9 seed. After defeating Sacramento in the 9-10 game, a heroic 40-ball sees them stun the Grizzlies to steal a playoff spot, only to get eviscerated by the powerhouse Thunder.

This turns out to be an utter disaster, as Cooper Flagg will no longer become a Maverick. It was possible to have a core of Brunson, Davis, and Flagg, but now? Brunson hits his 30th birthday with Davis shipped to Washington and a band of merrymen around him.

That’s right. The real twist of all of this? Nobody wins.

The Knicks lose because they don’t have Brunson. They never sniff the NBA Finals.

The Mavericks lose because the domino effect takes two lottery picks away, and JB’s hyper-competitiveness doesn’t allow them to get younger.

Jalen Brunson loses. Instead of being the King of New York, he’s got a microscope on him in lowly Dallas as the guy Nico traded Luka to feature.

It’s a lose-lose situation. What a nightmare. I need my nightlight; someone turn on some highlights.

That’s better. Happy Birthday, Cap. We’re so glad this never happened.

items.title: Happy 30th Birthday, Cap!
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Another Knick turns 30 this week! Days after Mikal Bridges reached the milestone, Captain Jalen Brunson celebrates his birthday today.

Born August 31, 1996, in New Brunswick, New Jersey, the Knicks captain hits the 30-year mark about 11 weeks after delivering New York its first NBA championship since 1973 and earning Finals MVP. Brunson capped the series with 45 points in the championship-clinching Game Five against the Spurs, a Knicks Finals record. Not a bad year so far, all things considered.

Brunson spent much of his childhood in southern New Jersey, including Cherry Hill, but his father’s basketball career kept the family moving. Rick Brunson played nine NBA seasons before transitioning to coaching, and the family eventually settled in the Chicago area, where Jalen attended Stevenson High School in Lincolnshire, Illinois. His mother, Sandra, played volleyball at Temple, where she and Rick were both student-athletes.

At Stevenson, Jalen won a state championship and Illinois Mr. Basketball honors. At Villanova, he won national championships in 2016 and 2018, then became the consensus National Player of the Year as a junior. Dallas selected him with the 33rd pick in the 2018 draft, making him the last of four Villanova teammates called—a fact most definitely not lost on the uber-competitive Jalen. Over his first four seasons, he developed from a reserve into a central figure on the Mavs team that reached the 2022 Western Conference Finals.

That summer, Jalen inked a four-year, $104 million contract with the Knickerbockers. The deal drew skepticism at the time, but Brunson quickly became the lead guard New York had spent decades seeking. He has since earned multiple All-Star and All-NBA selections, won the 2025 NBA Cup and its MVP award, and led the Knicks to the 2026 championship. On August 6, 2024, he became the 36th captain in franchise history.

Before Jalen arrived, the Knicks had made the playoffs once in the previous nine seasons. Four years later, they were champions. Rick had played for the 1998–99 Knicks, the franchise’s previous Finals team, and Jalen completed the circle by leading the orange-and-blue past the Spurs, the same team that defeated Rick’s Knicks.

The connections that brought Brunson to New York ran deep. Knicks president Leon Rose began his career as Rick’s agent and later represented Jalen. Tom Thibodeau had known Brunson since childhood through Rick’s NBA and coaching career, then hired Rick as an assistant in June 2022.

And the personal connections continue: the front office not only traded for Jalen’s BFF and Villanova teammate, Josh Hart, but also surrounded him with former teammates Bridges, Donte DiVincenzo, and Ryan Arcidiacono. Sometimes it seemed like Leon’s long game was less about Jalen and more about luring Jay Wright to the NBA.

Brunson practices his trade with strength, footwork, and deception. The 6-foot-2 left-hander changes pace, backs down larger defenders, pivots through traffic, and uses his body to create space. He absorbs contact, is a league leader in drawing charges, and is unafraid of smashing his way through much taller trees (especially French ones) or taking the game-winning shot as the clock expires. The steel in his veins and his big-shot helped make Captain Clutch the King of New York.

At 30, the mileage from that contact-heavy style will be worth monitoring, and coach Mike Brown may increasingly look for ways to preserve his champion. The injuries start to pile up as the seasons tick by: Jalen has suffered numerous ankle sprains, fractured his left hand during the 2024 playoffs, and played through a left wrist injury during the 2026 championship run before undergoing surgery in July. But his unparalleled craft should age better than a game dependent primarily on vertical explosiveness.

His 2024 extension includes a player option for 2028–29, allowing him to negotiate another contract before his 32nd birthday. By signing early rather than waiting for free agency, Jalen gave the Knicks the financial flexibility to build a championship-caliber roster around him. Reports estimated that decision left hay bales of money on the table, but he has trusted the organization to take care of him in time.

items.title: Westchester dates Knicks fans should circle
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Bummed out by the ticket prices at Madison Square Garden? Head over to the Westchester County Center in White Plains, where the jerseys look familiar and the seats are much more budget-friendly!

The Westchester Knicks released their complete 2026–27 schedule Friday. They open with two road games against the Maine Celtics on November 6 and November 8 before returning to their home gym to face the reigning G League champion Greensboro Swarm on November 14.

The G League season begins with a 14-game Tip-Off Tournament, with regional pods of teams playing one another. That leads into the Winter Showcase, held December 19–22 in Orlando, followed by a 36-game regular season in which every team’s record resets. Regular-season play begins around December 27.

You might be wondering whether G League games are as exciting as the big-league tilts. To which I counter: You would have had fun watching Tyler Kolek do this last season.

Here are a few games we’ll be zeroed in on during the 2026–27 campaign.

November 6 and 8 at Maine: Westchester immediately gets two games against Boston’s affiliate. The opening weekend should offer our first meaningful look at the Knicks’ developmental pecking order.

November 14 vs. Greensboro: The home opener gives us our first chance to see this roster in the flesh locally, while the Swarm arrive fresh off the first championship in franchise history.

Four early games against Long Island: Westchester faces Brooklyn’s affiliate twice during the Tip-Off Tournament and twice immediately after the regular-season reset. Four early games against the same opponent should provide a useful measuring stick, no?

January 18 and 20 vs. Cleveland: The Cavaliers’ affiliate comes to town for consecutive games, providing another useful glimpse at how Westchester compares with one of the Eastern Conference’s stronger developmental pipelines.

Three 11 a.m. School Day games: The annual chorus of several thousand children returns Wednesday, January 27; Tuesday, February 9; and Thursday, March 11. Bring earplugs.

The eventual assignments of Tyler Nickel, selected 47th in this summer’s NBA Draft, and New York’s other prospects will determine how closely we follow each date. Either way, I hope to see you at a few games this season.

items.title: Jose Alvarado believed, and now he’s an NBA champion
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
There are easier (and less surreal) ways to fulfill an NBA dream than the Jose Alvarado route.

Go undrafted and fight your way onto a roster. Develop a reputation as a defensive menace on the court. Spend four and a half seasons in NOLA. Get traded home to New York mid-season. Help your favorite team from childhood win their first championship in more than half a century. Then parade through the streets of the city where you grew up with a few million people screaming at you.

Alvarado sat down with SLAM during his cover shoot for KICKS 29, and the conversation naturally circled back to the improbable route that brought the Brooklyn native here.

Asked to choose one word for the Knicks’ championship run, Alvarado answered:  “Believe. That’s one thing you got to do is believe the way we did it.”

That was especially true in Game Four of the Finals, when New York fell 29 points behind San Antonio and somehow dragged itself all the way back, aided by significant contributions from Alvarado. He said his focus during the comeback was simple: “It was more not really overthinking—like, what can I do to make us win the game regardless if it’s making shots or not.”

The championship would have been a massive achievement anywhere. Winning it in New York meant even more for Jose, who grew up in Brooklyn before playing at Georgia Tech and eventually joining the Pelicans.

Pondering Jose’s experience, there is always something weird about getting a desperately wanted thing. For years, the dream existed at a distance, beyond the next practice, the next contract, the doubt expressed by others about your size or talent. Then one afternoon, you’re dancing on a float in Manhattan as an NBA champion with your hometown passing by, block by block. 

“I almost cried on the float because . . . obviously going through the city that I was raised . . . I know a lot of people that’s in the crowd,” Alvarado told SLAM.

That’s the part of winning a championship nobody can really prepare for, that transition point when the dream stops being something you’re chasing and becomes something that has happened to you. Sounds surreal. And not to get all Jean-Paul Sartre about it all, but it’s natural to wonder: what’s next?

The answer: Your own sneaker and a new contract with the Knicks, naturally. After declining his $4.5 million player option this summer, Alvarado agreed to a new three-year deal with the Knicks worth roughly $14.4 million, with $12 million guaranteed.

Furthermore, Jose recently signed with the streetball brand AND1 and showed off his personalized player-exclusive shoes during the SLAM shoot. The partnership makes sense. Few NBA players have built an identity more closely connected to playground basketball’s particular mixture of hustle, swagger, annoyance, and joy. Thus, the SLAM team drove Alvarado back to an outdoor New York court, a familiar environment to the 28-year-old who is currently playing for Puerto Rico in FIFA’s Basketball World Cup qualifiers.

In March, I spoke to Jose over Zoom. He was connecting from a hotel room in Utah, grinding out NBA life on the road, still getting acclimated to his new team. What struck me in the conversation was how completely disruptive a mid-season trade is on a player with a young family. 

“People don’t understand,” Alvarado told me. “You think, ‘They’ve got millions,’ and don’t get me wrong, the financial security is great. But one day you’re comfortable in your forever home, and overnight you have to go to a different city, leaving your wife and kids behind.”

He explained that even a month after the trade, he hadn’t yet been able to return home to his family in New Orleans. It became clear how much these players—and their families—must sacrifice for an NBA career.

And Jose is not slowing down. Despite the ring, a new contract, and his face on a SLAM cover, Alvarado doesn’t sound particularly interested in staying comfortable.

“The only way to stay in the NBA, or to be in a conversation where I want to be, with my goal, is [I] definitely got to have a chip on my shoulder, no matter what,” he told SLAM.

That chip is mighty durable. Going undrafted didn’t remove it; making an NBA team didn’t shake it; becoming an established rotation player didn’t loosen it; and neither did coming home, getting paid, or getting to pose for glamour shots with the Larry O’Brien trophy.

Asked how he eventually wants people to remember him, Jose went right back to the beginning. “I want them to remember that there was a lot of people that said no to this kid. There was a lot of doubts . . . just remember the doubts and how I overcame all that.”

I can think of worse epitaphs for a basketball career. Congrats, Jose.

items.title: Friday Posted & Toasted Notes: International Knicks, KD & Dray & T-Mac talk too much
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
I let everybody down not publishing notes in a week, thinking there was nothing happening around the League but still saving clippings into a document that ended up growing monstrous. Won’t happen again, for my own health.

  • Jalen Brunson’s wrist recovery remains the biggest health variable hanging over the Knicks. Dexter Henry of the New York Post stressed the difference between Brunson being medically cleared and actually looking like Brunson again, while Bryan Fonseca argued that New York’s repeat hopes effectively disappear if its Finals MVP cannot return to his pre-injury level. All we know is that Brunson is still not participating in basketball activities and has described the rehab process as “frustrating.”
  • James L. Edwards III of The Athletic has heard estimates ranging from roughly $54-$62 million over three years for Hart’s next deal, although Edwards believes something closer to $70-$80 million might represent fairer value.
  • Hart spoke to our own Michael Zeno and opened up about how much New York has come to feel like home after years of bouncing around the league. Hart also revealed he has no plans to undergo another procedure on the troublesome ring finger of his shooting hand despite playing through the injury last season.

“But now, I’m in New York. I feel like I have a home here, and I’m extremely happy.”

“No, I’ll let it go. At the end of my career, when I’m done hooping, I’ll probably have to get a joint replacement in it, but for now it’s fine.”

  • Hart offered a nice explanation for what keeps him grounded through an NBA season, mentioned his wife, Mikal Bridges and Brunson as people who help him navigate the grind and, in perhaps Hart’s best reflection on the championship he just won, he said roughly 90 percent of fans who approach him mention either their father or their son when discussing the title. Worth read in full!
  • Jose Alvarado kept his dream year going, now internationally. The Brooklyn-born Knicks guard is representing Puerto Rico at the FIBA World Cup, and he already scored a team-high 19 points for Puerto Rico in an 89-75 World Cup qualifying loss to Argentina. The Knicks guard shot 7-of-15 from the field and added six rebounds and four assists. Former Knick Pablo Prigioni coached Argentina.
  • Pacome Dadiet, who does not represent France, also made his senior international debut, helping Ivory Coast beat Mali 83-77. Dadiet scored nine points on 4-of-12 shooting and struggled from deep at 1-of-8, but grabbed a game-high nine rebounds, including five on the offensive glass.
  • The Knicks’ third-center search took another hit with Nick Richards going to the Miami Heat. With Ariel Hukporti already gone to Philadelphia and Mitchell Robinson in Boston, New York still has not filled the final, third-string center spot behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond. The increasingly likely outcome? A training-camp competition between veterans on non-guaranteed deals to determine he earns the gig.
  • The Knicks, meanwhile, still have all three two-way roster spots open with training camp approaching. Rookie Tyler Nickel remains unsigned and could fill one of them if he begins his professional career rather than returning to college.
  • Leon Rose received major praise from CBS Sports’ Sam Quinn for building one of the strangest championship rosters in league history, as the Knicks just became only the second NBA champion ever to win without drafting a single member of its starting five, joining the 2020 Lakers.
  • The Athletic’s latest NBA power rankings put the Knicks at No. 1 overall entering training camp.

“It’s easy to put the Knicks at No. 1 after their dominant postseason run. Ten of their top 12 players return, though NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson has to recover from wrist surgery on his shooting hand. Drummond replaces Robinson, but the team still doesn’t have a replacement for Hukporti. We know the Knicks want to replace Hukporti, because they signed center Moussa Cissé to an offer sheet that the Dallas Mavericks matched.

“The regular season will be interesting for the defending champs. There hasn’t been a dominant regular-season Knicks team in the 21st century, as the Knicks haven’t won at least 55 games since 1996-97. Will that matter? How many regular-season losses would it take before we start to believe the Knicks might not be a repeat threat come April? Those are the real questions.” — Law Murray

  • (Not) shockingly, ESPN’s summer forecast is much less convinced the Knicks will repeat. Its panel picked New York to win the Eastern Conference with 68 points, comfortably ahead of Philadelphia at 51… but ranked the Knicks a distant third in NBA championship voting behind Oklahoma City and San Antonio. The Thunder received 84 points, the Spurs 74 and New York only 11.
  • DeMar DeRozan is headed to Denver on a one-year, $3.9 million deal after being waived by Sacramento. Meanwhile, Klay Thompson officially joined Miami after clearing waivers following a buyout with Dallas.
  • Jonathan Kuminga finally found a home, agreeing with Minnesota on a two-year contract that includes a player option.
  • Kevin Durant called the Knicks’ championship run “the best championship as a viewer that I’ve ever seen.”

“I was on the fence on if they were going to win. And then they got down every game, and I’m just like, ‘I don’t know.’ And then they started coming back. I didn’t become a believer, to be honest, until the last game. I was just like, the Spurs would be up 15 points every game, 29 points, and then they’d just come back and steal a game. That’s probably why that was the best championship as a viewer that I’ve ever seen.

“Not just because of the Knicks brand winning, but just the fashion they won those games in, it was insane. It really showed you the power dynamic in the NBA: a veteran team that was put together through trades vs. a team that drafted everybody that a lot of people would have loved to see win. For the Knicks to do it that way, I felt they made a statement.”

  • Durant also weighed in on Jalen Brunson’s decision to leave roughly $100 million on the table, acknowledging he understands why Brunson made the sacrifice and credited the move for helping New York build a championship roster. That said, KD admitted he probably would have been talked out of doing the same.

“I understand his thought process and why he actually executed that. I can’t put myself in that position and just say, ‘Yeah, I would have done it or not.’ For him to make that decision and come out the way it did, kudos to him. But hopefully he gets that back on the back end.

“I would have gotten talked out of it. I probably would have been like, ‘All right, I’m cool with it.’ I’d have sat down and talked to all my people like I usually do, Rich, all my friends. Like, ‘What? Are you serious? Why do you need to take that risk when this dude’s a billionaire?’ Nobody would do that.”

  • Draymond Green likes Klay Thompson’s move to Miami but wonders how the famously independent Thompson will mesh with “Heat Culture.”
  • Green also pushed back against treating the signing as though Miami is getting 2018 Klay, comparing the move more appropriately to Ray Allen joining the Heat late in his career.

“I don’t like how everybody’s trying to act like, ‘Oh man, it’s Klay Thompson’ like Klay to the Heat, like this is Klay of 2018. The reason I don’t like it is because I feel like everybody’s trying to set Klay up for failure. And so, I’m going to say it right here, right now. Let’s stop acting like 2017 Klay is going to Miami.

“Don’t try to set my brother up like you about to get the 2017 Klay, so the moment you don’t, y’all can bash him. That’s bullsh*t. He’s going into Year 16 of his career. We obviously know the injuries that he’s faced.”

  • Tracy McGrady offered another contribution to the endless rings-versus-individual-awards debate, arguing that a regular-season MVP carries more weight than winning a championship. Sheesh…
  • Ice Cube remains convinced BIG3 players should represent the United States in Olympic 3-on-3 basketball, calling USA Basketball “crazy” for not using what he believes are the best 3-on-3 players in the country. And he’s damn right.

“They’re crazy not to use our athletes as the U.S. Olympic team in 3-on-3. The last two Olympics have been a disaster for USA when it comes to what USA Basketball has been putting together to represent the US. I hope they have a ‘come-to-Jesus moment’ and realize that we have the best 3-on-3 players in the world. It’s not even close. They should use our athletes to represent the U.S., especially on U.S. soil. Will they do that or not? Egos may win and prevail, and the U.S. will suffer because of that.”

  • Blake Griffin is moving into late-night television, starting on Oct. 20.
  • Metta Sandiford-Artest attempted to buy a one-percent stake in the Lakers for $100 million but was swiftly turned down.

items.title: What should the Knicks do with a Karl-Anthony Towns extension?
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
As we go deeper into the dog days of the offseason, the Knicks are a team with relatively few questions. After all, they just won the title (still feels great to say that) and returned almost all of their production from that title run, but there are still things to discuss as we patiently wait for more basketball on our screens.

High up on that list of things pertains to a potential contract extension for a player whose postseason buy-in was unlike anything we’ve seen before on both ends, who had a real case to win Finals MVP before the league mandate to both extend the series and prop up Wemby forced him into repeated foul trouble to end the series.

That’s, of course, Karl-Anthony Towns.

No player, not even Jalen Brunson or OG Anunoby, has experienced a better PR boost from this title than Towns. The median NBA fan would call Towns an overpaid, zesty (whatever that means), defensive liability to undermine just how dominant an offensive player he is, but his defensive buy-in and versatility as an offensive engine for a dominant playoff run changed hearts and minds. He’s now unanimously considered a top 15 player in the game.

But how should said player be paid? Handsomely, surely, but it’s more complicated than that.

It’s 2026, and although player empowerment is by far the social norm, there have been considerable efforts to curtail it, particularly with the current CBA and the introduction of the second apron.

It’s meant to give players a proposition. You can either make what you want or have a sustainable winner. If you get the max contract, you’ll be taking money away from your supporting cast, which will decrease your odds of winning a championship. If you take less money, you’d be getting paid less than some guys who clearly don’t deserve to be in your same tax bracket.

Brunson is a perfect example. He could’ve waited a year and signed a five-year, $269 million mega-extension in 2025, but elected to take four years and $156 million a year early for a myriad of reasons. If he wanted to make the most money, he likely wouldn’t have gotten a co-star in KAT, given the team’s aversion to the second apron. Role players like Jose Alvarado wouldn’t be here. Big moves would be made year after year to fit a few specific salaries, preventing the team from geling properly.

But while his extension has brought him the ultimate glory and likely earned him a massive future extension, it didn’t come without risk. Beyond the fact that there’s no guarantee he would’ve been given another big extension if he regressed in the ensuing four years, he was now making less than guys like Desmond Bane, LaMelo Ball, Michael Porter Jr., Darius Garland, Domantas Sabonis, Ja Morant, Zach LaVine, Paul George, and more. He’s the 47th highest-paid player in 2026-27, despite being a top-five player in the game. These guys can’t lace his boots.

Towns can do the same thing that his co-star did: take less money, but should he? Unlike Brunson, who was entering his age-28 season when he signed it, KAT is going to be 31 in November. The extension would start when he’s 32 and likely take him through age 36, when, barring LeBron-esque longevity, he’ll be diminished. This will be his last big paycheck.

The max he is eligible for this offseason is a huge sum of four years and $272 million. That’s $68 million a year. His current 2027-28 salary is a player option worth $61 million, so based on the contract escalators, he wouldn’t make too much more, but it would put him on the books for north of $70 million into his mid-30s. While the salary cap will continue to rise and make it less of an issue, that’s a lot of money for a player exiting his prime.

It’s also inhibitive of roster construction, particularly if James Dolan continues to drag his feet over even one season of the second apron. The Knicks currently have $226 million of salary on the books for 2027-28 with 10 players rostered, sitting just $7 million under the projected second apron. Any raise for Towns against his player option would be prohibitive and make it impossible to stay under the second apron without trades, particularly if the team has any desire to keep a guy like Deuce McBride.

The Knicks already won their championship, so the team should be in a state of enjoying the riches that they’ve earned, but it’s not 2018 anymore, when Joe Lacob was just able to spend infinite money on maintaining his superteam with no roster restrictions. Dolan has the money, which is what makes the decision even more bizarre, particularly when the repeater tax does not apply until next season. If there was any year to go into that second apron, it was this year, so I have my doubts he’ll do it next year.

The Knicks should extend KAT. He, like Brunson and Anunoby and maybe more, should go down as a Knicks legend and either retire here or be defined by their tenures here. If he merely plays out his contract, Towns will spend just three (or four) years as a Knick, a tenure that is dwarfed by his near-decade in Minnesota. The guy who’s the first star center to lift the Larry O’Brien in the orange and blue since Willis Reed should be remembered as a Knick, plain and simple.

That’s going to have to come with some sacrifice, though, and that sucks. We’re at an unprecedented point where a team is going to have to ask an All-NBA talent to take less money winning a championship, and ask isn’t even a strong enough word. If he doesn’t take less, this core will likely begin to be disassembled next offseason.

So what’s the sweet spot? How much would both properly pay the Big Bodega for his contributions while also allowing this team and this core to get as many bites of the apple at a second championship as possible?

I thought about this for a good bit, and ultimately came out to a four-year pact worth about $230 million, shaving $42 million off the top of Towns’ max for an average annual value of $57.5 million. It might be a tough ask for a guy as valuable as KAT to take eight figures less per year, but let me show my work.

This would give Towns a Year 1 salary of approximately $50 million, which is $11 million less than his 2027-28 player option. While certainly a tough pill for him to swallow, it would make him anywhere from the 12th to 17th highest-paid player in basketball, depending on the exact dollar amount ($50.3m would put him 12th, for example). That’s fair money, even if the guys in his range aren’t worth it (Jamal Murray, Evan Mobley, Paul George).

The bigger emphasis here, though, is roster building. By saving $11 million, the Knicks would suddenly be $18 million beneath the second apron with five open roster spots in 2027-28, giving them more than enough money to stay beneath the threshold, albeit still with losing McBride. There’s at least a path to retaining McBride with some creative financing (and maybe a cheaper Hart extension) by declining Pacome Dadiet’s team option, which would put the team over $23 million beneath the apron.

As the extension progresses, Towns would make $54 million in 2028-29, $58.3 million in 2029-30, and $63 million in 2030-31, which would likely be a player option. Deducing financials from this point would depend on other moves, particularly with Shamet and Alvarado’s team-friendly, partially guaranteed extensions, but also whether McBride or Hart get a new contract.

I’d be surprised if he went into this season without an extension, mostly just because I expect nothing in-season and it’d be shocking to see him deal with those rumors all season with a player option looming. We’ve seen it happen with a bunch of other players, but KAT doesn’t strike me as that kind of guy.

Training camp will be fun.

items.title: His name is Enes Kanter
items.author: Matthew Miranda
items.content:
Not a lot broke right for David Fizdale’s 2019 Knicks, but if a broke clock is right twice a day that’s 730 times a year, so even Fiz had his moments. One came a few months into another lost season, after he got over the shock of Kevin Durant and Zion Williamson not walking through that door, looked around the locker room and decided the Knicks’ future centered on its two young centers, Mitchell Robinson and Luke Kornet. That pair went on to play supporting roles as backup bigs for NBA champions. The center they displaced did not.

Enes Kanter’s postseason history is short and direct, like a shiv. He was Oklahoma City’s only real reserve big man in 2016, what with Kevin Durant, Serge Ibaka and Steven Adams each playing 30-40 minutes per playoff game. Three years later, Kanter was the starting center for a Portland side that made the Western finals before being swept by Golden State. The next season he played bit minutes for Boston the first two rounds before barely seeing the floor in the ECF vs. Miami. Spoiler: Kanter existing right as the NBA downshifted to pace-and-space and 3s was like the dinosaurs existing the same time as the asteroid. Tough break.

Fizdale likely figured Kanter — older, more worldly and presumably more mature than Kornet or Mitch, three and six years his juniors — would handle the news with grace. Brace yourself: Fizdale was wrong.

“For me to get to the next level, just be a good teammate, support my teammate out there and clap for him and cheer for him,’’ Kanter said at the time. “I’ll go out and do my job and help my team win. If we’re winning, it’s good. But if we’re losing it’s a problem. If this adjustment is going to get us a win, cool. But if not, there’s a problem.”

There’s a problem all right. Not that I’m surprised Kanter could both state it and miss it, simultaneously.

He changed his name years ago, because like the bottle-blonde Leavitts and low-T-hating Hegseths of the world, Kanter has no sense of shame. He’s open publicly about changes he’s made to his identity to better reflect the way he wishes to be seen by others. But as one who literally hugs the flag fails to recognize what such a slovenly act says about them, Kanter isn’t merely lacking in self-awareness. Self-awareness is entirely beside the point. Because “Enes Freedom” really isn’t about freedom. Which is sad.

For years, Kanter has been an outspoken critic of Turkish dictator Recep Erdoğan. The personal may be political, but it’s often the other way around, too. Born in Switzerland, Kanter gained Turkish citizenry through his parents. He’s endured Erdoğan’s forces imprisoning and oppressing his loved ones in Turkey and escaped a Turkish kidnapping attempt in Indonesia, so you can see how even a man bigger than Charles Oakley could be scared. He’s only human; he wasn’t looking to become a political target. You can understand why he sought American citizenship, understand him saying, “I feel like this is my home now.”

The D.C. kleptocracy abhors Europe in general and birthright citizenship in particular, so you might not expect them to view Kanter fondly, nor he them. Yet hate makes for strange bedfellows, so wealthy, anonymous powers-that-be fly their willing human cargo to Chicago with primo seats for a Sky game, claiming he’s there to “support women.” That manifested as Kanter going harder and louder after the Sky’s Natalie Cloud than he ever did Royce White. White recently joined Kanter in “supporting women” by facetiously stating their intent to enter the WNBA draft, after which we learned White’s ex-wife and the mother of his son was granted a 50-year order of protection after years of White’s abuse and intimidation.

It was the same story with Damyean Dotson, Kanter’s former Knick teammate who faced rape charges while at the University of Oregon. The district attorney’s office dropped the case, though not without stating “there is no doubt the incidents occurred [ . . . ] the conflicting statements and actions by the victim make this case unprovable as a criminal case.” The victim won a settlement from the school after a case that saw Dotson’s defense peddle in the pathetic, including the claim that “because the University [sic] disciplines male students for sexual misconduct but never female students, it is biased against men.” Hospitals treat the sick but never the healthy, therefore they’re biased. 

And who among us doesn’t remember where they were the first time they heard Kanter’s impassioned support for women after Michael Beasley was accused of stripping, choking and raping a woman? Or wait — was that after Kyle O’Quinn allegedly punched a woman? Or Kristaps Porziņģis was accused of rape? Kanter’s former teammate Ime Udoka cheated on his wife with a woman in the Celtics organization, who unless she’s the owner’s wife is by default less powerful within the Celtics than Udoka was as the head coach. Oh, to have been a fly on the wall when Kanter let Udoka have it after being personally and professionally in the red.

Plenty of opportunities to support women by punching up. The 49ers owner was arrested this week for soliciting prostitution from an undercover cop. One of the football Giants’ owners is more than a little linked with Jeffrey Epstein’s child rape racket. James Dolan forces facial recognition technology on millions of unwitting people. Kanter thinks he’s edgy for bugging Cloud at her job.

“Never, ever hide,” Kanter told Fox News in a 2023 interview. “Hiding is not an option. I know it can be a bit dangerous sometimes, but . . . we live in a free country.” Not everybody, Enes. Yesterday in Connecticut, ICE waited for school kids to get on the morning bus, then kidnapped their parents. The cruelty was the point: when the kids get home after school, they can’t find their parents and have no idea what’s happened to them, nor where to search without subjecting themselves to the same cruel system. ICE shoots and kills women in the face. They rape and kill women in their concentration camps.

Contrast that with the article photo: literally, angry man yells at Cloud. That night, Kanter’s head hit the pillow with him proudly centered as both hero and victim. The kind of man a woman would rather avoid than a bear.

I won’t call him Enes Freedom anymore. Freedom means sharing the rights and responsibilities you demand for yourself with those you live with and around. Escaping oppression, only to pile on some other oppressed people, is not freedom. That’s impunity. After a string of DNPs near the end of his days in New York, Kanter kissed the Garden floor after finally returning to action. “Obviously, on the court and off the court I’ve been having a very rough time the last three weeks with Turkey issues and basketball issues,” he said. “The support that they are showing just meant a lot to me.”

items.title: The Bruiser Refusing the Final Buzzer: Charles Oakley, MSG, and The Last Enforcer
items.author: John Gove
items.content:
The recent dismissal of Charles Oakley’s long-running lawsuit against Madison Square Garden marks a brutal collision between the unwritten code of loyalty and the court’s objective reality. For a third time, Judge Richard J. Sullivan of the Southern District of New York dismissed Oakley’s remaining assault and battery claims. The nine-year battle stemming from the infamous ejection in February 2017 consistently ends the same way. However, for anyone who has read , the legal defeats barely explain the feud’s full scope.

Oakley’s memoir serves as an oral history of moral correctness, providing the context for why a retired player refuses to let an almost decade-old legal dispute rest, even as mounting losses and legal fees pile up. Reading the book alongside Judge Sullivan’s latest ruling highlights an interesting contrast. It pins the reality of the American judicial system against the stubborn, emotional pride of a basketball enforcer.

To understand this endless litigation, we have to look back at the era of basketball Oakley helped define and the specific role he carved out. Throughout his memoir, Oakley discusses his time under Pat Riley and Jeff Van Gundy. During the 90s, he established himself as the alpha bodyguard, specifically for Patrick Ewing. He describes willingly sacrificing his body to shield his teammates from harm on the court and scrutiny of New York’s media. He constructed the blue-collar intimidator identity that defined 90s Eastern Conference basketball.

The irony of his current situation is painful. The sacrificial dynamic Oakley details in his book contrasts with his current standing with the Knicks organization. The man who bled to defend his team is now treated as a hostile trespasser by the franchise he protected. He draws a direct line between how the franchise treats its legends and its corporate culture. Oakley argues that the organization as a whole does not respect the players who built the foundation.

Unsurprisingly, Oak pulls no punches when discussing James Dolan. Throughout the book, he portrays him as a privileged figure with thin skin who demands compliance. Oakley strongly claims the Knicks owner abuses his power, holding grudges against anyone who dares to criticize him or the team. For Oakley, the ejection from MSG was never about legal statutes. Instead, it was about standing up to a bully who used arena security to settle a personal vendetta. What makes the book’s portrayal so compelling is how MSG’s actual corporate behavior mirrors Oakley’s narrative. After the recent ruling, MSG didn’t simply issue a standard public statement. Instead, they went on the offensive, declaring their intention to pursue legal action against Oakley’s attorney, Douglas Wigdor, and his firm, accusing them of “frivolous litigation” and “blatant abuse of the judicial system.” This combative retaliation illustrates what Oakley continuously revisits in his memoir.

While Oakley succeeds in painting himself as a marginalized hero battling the corporate monster, courts do not operate by locker-room codes. They stick to evidence, which repeatedly dismantles Charles Oakley’s claims. Judge Sullivan provided a definitive ruling, noting that ample evidence proved the Knicks legend was never pushed to the ground. It stated that Oakley had a reasonable opportunity to leave The Garden peacefully but resorted to physical violence instead. Sullivan also concluded that no rational jury would find that security intentionally created fear or unlawful contact.

For the former power forward, the legal reality of this whole circumstance has been quite costly. Beyond having his claims dismissed three separate times, the litigation has carried a steep financial burden. In 2025, a judge ordered Oakley to pay nearly $642,000 in attorney fees and costs related to MSG’s efforts to recover deleted text messages after the incident. Unfortunately for Oak, the evidence and the judicial system have unquestionably sided with Dolan and the Knicks organization.

Despite the defeats, Enforcer’s primary theme explains what takes place next. The same stubbornness and refusal to back down that made Charles Oakley a beloved legend is what keeps him appealing the lawsuit. Whether it’s on the basketball court or in the courtroom, he does not know how to back down from a fight.

Just one day after the most recent dismissal, Oakley used Instagram to display a photo from his playing days, adding “#ItsNotOver” and “#JuryTrial.” To complement the Instagram post, his legal team has already indicated its intention to appeal to the Second Circuit Court again. Though unlikely, they hope to get a jury trial this time around.

This whole ordeal marks the tragedy of an enforcer who fails to hear the final buzzer. While the court issued a definitive ruling, the friction between Oakley’s narrative and MSG’s aggressive postering ensures this messy dispute isn’t over. Concluding whether Charles Oakley’s legacy will be defined by his on-court enforcement or this endless legal battle remains a complicated discussion, potentially creating more divisiveness before it’s through.

items.title: Josh Hart talks Scouting America ambassadorship, championship run
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The champs have been busy this offseason, continuing their media tours with new sponsorships, talk shows, and overall just enjoying the best few months anyone could ask for as kings of their respective worlds.

The extra media attention has given us some pretty cool opportunities at P&T. Kento talked to Karl-Anthony Towns last month, Russ got a chance to talk to the ever-mysterious OG Anunoby, and I got the opportunity to talk to everyone’s favorite glue guy, Josh Hart, as part of his recent ambassadorship announcement with , formerly known as “Boy Scouts of America”.

Hart was in the Scouts program for much of his childhood, joining it to follow in the footsteps of his older brother, Moses, and one of his close friends. He gradually rose through the ranks before putting it off at age 13 as life and basketball started to pick up for him. At 16, he returned to the program at the wish of his father, who wanted him to keep his years-old promise to see things through. Josh eventually earned the rank of Eagle Scout, the highest honor, a week before his 18th birthday.

When asked why he decided now to be an ambassador for the program that shaped much of his upbringing, Hart cited what the program meant for him growing up.

“It’s always been an uphill climb in my career, but I’ve always had life lessons that I’ve gotten from Scouting, and I think now is a good time to partner with them and try to influence other kids, parents, adults, and tell them, you know, you can do both.”

“You can do sports, you can do arts, you can do engineering, or whatever walk of life you want to do as a kid, but you can also do Scouting,” he added. “You don’t have to pick between one or the other.”

I followed up by asking him about that sort of balance that he mentioned of being able to do both Scouting and pursue things like basketball, as he did growing up. For him, it was about time management and sacrifice.

“The big thing is sacrifice,” Hart said. “There’s going to be times you might not be able to hang out with friends, or there might be times when you can’t go to a camping trip or a basketball camp or a football camp. There’s going to be sacrifices, but as long as you’re good with managing the time and saying, ‘I got to do X for this merit badge; I got to put the work in on the court this week. Let me lock in for this.’ You’ll put yourself in the best position to be successful.”

Scouting wasn’t for me, personally, growing up. I tried it once because one of my close friends was super into it, but it just didn’t stick for me. A lot of people I know learned valuable lessons there, so it was nice to pick the brain of someone who went through the system and has applied what he’s learned to everyday life and, particularly, his role as a “glue guy” in the NBA.

“You have to have that teamwork mentality,” Hart said about applying his lessons in Scouting to his basketball career. “It’s not always about you, and sometimes that’s hard to realize, but Scouting helps you understand that more and more.”

“You can’t be out on a trail, 15-20 miles from civilization, when someone gets hurt and think about yourself, he added. ” You’ve got to make sure you’re not focused on yourself, but on how you can help this person, how you can help the group, and navigate where you are and the dangers. I think that [Scouting] definitely helped with the foundation of being a servant.“

The purpose of this interview was to, of course, shed light on Josh’s ambassadorship, but we’d be remiss not to talk ball. I first asked him a question about both Scouting and basketball, giving him a chance to make a basketball merit badge, which he said would require being able to “dribble, shoot, have lateral quickness, leadership”, while adding that the latter aspect would be earned through certain game situations. I can think of a guy who’d get this badge quite easily.

We got some physical media attached to the interview opportunity, which came with the following image of Hart doing the Boy Scout sign, which entails raising three fingers on your right hand. See if you can find what piqued my interest here:

The ring finger on his shooting hand was a topic of discussion in Knicks circles all season long, particularly when he had his low points from the perimeter. He underwent a procedure on the finger after the 2024-25 season, but aggravated it during training camp, electing to play through it with a splint all of the following season. With the finger still appearing to be busted, I asked if he had any plans to repair it, whether now or in the future:

“No, I’ll let it go,” Hart said. “At the end of my career, when I’m done hooping, I’ll probably have to get a joint replacement in it, but for now it’s fine.”

He agreed with my subsequent comment about not messing with what’s working, and I can see why. Hart notably shot a career-high 41.3 percent from downtown on reasonable volume, attempting 3.7 per game. Game 2 against Cleveland was a perfect example of how he didn’t let the injury impact his efficiency:

I stayed away from asking about Hart’s contract situation, in which he’s currently eligible for an extension with a team option currently on the books for 2027-28, but I asked about what it’s been like to have stability in New York, particularly after winning a title and seemingly entrenching the core of this team even further.

“When you’re young in the league, you’re trying to prove yourself and have a long career in the league, and that gets harder and harder the more you’re moving around,” he remarked before adding that he was always traded for a star prior to coming to NY. “It’s tough to try to solidify yourself when you’re going from team to team. Before I came to New York, I had six different coaches in my six years in the league, so it was tough.”

“But now, I’m in New York. I feel like I have a home here, and I’m extremely happy.”

Before getting to the good stuff about the championship, I also touched on the slog of an NBA season and how a guy like him, renowned for his tremendous hustle, sticks with it over the course of the season.

“I think it’s family, obviously my wife is a huge part of that, I’m with her almost every day, so she always keeps me grounded,” he said, touching on a few things that keep him in it. “Having close friends on the team—Mikal, JB— me and JB sit on the plane, so we talk about a lot of game or family stuff, so there’s that, but also my faith.”

“Friends, family, faith, those are the three ‘F’s’ that ground me and help me through tough times, whether that’s tough times on the court or off the court.”

His Twitter feed is always entertaining, but what stood out this week was the rehashing of that moment in Game 4, where the Knicks were on the verge of taking their first lead after the 29-point comeback on a steal and a Hart breakaway, but he missed the layup before committing a foul on the other end. After the whistle blew, he sat frustrated on the ground, only for his teammates to help him up and keep him focused on the end goal.

“They just told me to get up and move on,” Hart said about that moment. “Jose, KAT, JB, pick me up. You can see Landry yelling and motioning for me to get up, and I think that just shows the togetherness we had, where it’s like, ‘Okay, there was a mistake, but now let’s regroup, let’s figure out how we’re going to overcome that mistake and persevere in the moment.’”

“I think that just shows the tight-knit culture and team that we had, and I think that’s a big reason why we won.”

Lastly, I wanted to ask him about what it’s been like to essentially achieve basketball nirvana. It was said for decades that when big stars were linked to the Knicks, “Just imagine what winning a title there will do for their legacy.” How they’ll never have to pay for a meal again in the greatest city in the world. To be elevated beyond the pantheon of champions to being forever beloved in the city that never sleeps.

He used that opportunity to talk about what’s it felt to feel that kind of love by directing it back at the fans and seeing what it means to them.

“The thing that’s super cool for me is that about 90 percent of the people that have talked to me about it, they always mentioned either their dad or their son, and I think that’s the coolest thing.”

“You never want to have a 53-year-long championship drought, but that’s generations. There are people who’s dad’s watched 1973 who were waiting for another one and raised their kids to be Knicks fans, and now they watch those games together. It’s so cool, because it really seemed like it just united families; it gave families that thing throughout all of New York, so it was super cool to hear that.”

That part really hit home with me, even as someone who’s too young to have witnessed the Patrick Ewing era, let alone the ancient (in basketball terms) championships in the 1970s. The second the buzzer sounded in Game 5, I immediately hugged my 39-year-old brother, who’s the reason I became a Knicks fan. He was alive for the 90s; he was alive to see all the pain and failure from the 2000s and early 2010s while I was way too young to understand the game like I do today.

It’s really a powerful moment to have decades of heartbreak spill out, and it’s nice to know that the people who provided us with this happiness that some never thought would come appreciate the love the same way we appreciate them for ending a decades-long nightmare.

items.title: On This Date in Knicks History: Julius Randle re-commits to New York
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Ahhh, the 2020–21 season. I remember it well. After years as a punchline, the Knicks unexpectedly became competitive under first-year, veteran coach Tom Thibodeau and breakout star Julius Randle. They finished with a winning record, earned the fourth seed in the Eastern Conference, and returned to the postseason.

Randle’s stellar season (24.1 points, 10.2 rebounds, six assists, All-Star, second-team All-NBA, Most Improved Player) helped the team go from the butt of jokes to something more competent. He was high-usage, physical, available, and visibly invested in the work ethic Thibs demanded. Randle defined the season on April 21, 2021 when—after scoring 40 points and grabbing 11 boards to beat the Hawks in overtime—he famously told the MSG crowd, “We here.”

We loved it, this weird, slippery feeling he brought back to us called . The Knicks lost to the Hawks in the first round, but we were undeterred. For the first time in a long time, the hope felt real.

Randle was taken seventh in the 2014 draft by the Lakers. Take a look at how young and unrefined he was back in 2019, at his first media day as a Knickerbocker. He would come a long way in a short time under the bright lights of NYC.

On August 25, 2021, Randle signed a four-year extension worth a reported $117 million with incentives and a player option in the final year. It was the most the Knicks could offer under CBA rules, but a sight less than Randle might have earned by reaching unrestricted free agency in 2022. Had he maintained something close to his All-NBA production, projections put his next deal near five years and $200 million. (I’d love to know how he explained that to Mrs. Randle.)

Randle justified leaving tens of millions on the table by saying he believed the decision would give the Knicks greater flexibility to build a contender. After earlier career stops with the Lakers and Pelicans, where he had not always been happy, Jules wanted to lock into a situation he believed in. The big fella received security, continuity, and a chance to help shape the franchise. And the fanbase received an encouraging sign that sophomore team president Leon Rose was committed to building around what the Knicks already had rather than waiting for a free-agent savior.

The immediate results were a tad worrying, however. Randle regressed in 2021–22, and the Knicks missed the playoffs. The frustration peaked on January 6, 2022, against Boston at Madison Square Garden. After the Knicks fell behind by 25 and heard boos from the crowd, Randle responded to a fourth-quarter bucket with a thumbs-down gesture. Asked afterward what it meant, he replied, “Shut the f*** up.” He later apologized on Instagram, and the NBA fined him $25,000 for the language.

There are many reasons that season went off the rails, including the gamble on Kemba Walker’s knees and the mixed results from Evan Fournier. Randle’s prominence on the team, his mood swings, and his drop in production made him the most obvious target for fans who, less than a year earlier, had such high hopes. There’s that word again, the slippery bastard.

Nevertheless, the organization did not regress into perpetual reconstruction. Thibodeau’s culture of toughness and accountability took root around Randle and holdovers such as RJ Barrett and Mitchell Robinson. The Knicks had begun to resemble a credible basketball operation again, and that mattered in 2022, when they cleared cap space and signed Jalen Brunson to a four-year, $104 million deal.

Brunson quickly became the primary creator and eventual face of the franchise (and captain!). Randle adapted to playing alongside him, producing additional All-Star and All-NBA seasons. Success followed.

The Knicks became regular playoff participants while improving the roster through savvy front-office moves. Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, and eventually Mikal Bridges joined the group. Then, in October 2024, Randle’s part of the story ended. New York sent him, Donte DiVincenzo, Keita Bates-Diop, and a first-round pick to Minnesota in the three-team trade for Karl-Anthony Towns.

The front office publicly thanked Randle for helping establish the foundation and culture, and the trade showed how far the franchise had advanced. New York could exchange one accomplished All-NBA player for another whose skill set better suited the roster around Brunson. Towns brought size, shooting, and secondary creation to a starting five reinforced by Anunoby, Bridges, and Hart.

That group eventually reached the mountaintop Randle never could as a Knick. Thibodeau was replaced by Mike Brown, who coached the 2025–26 squad to 53 wins, an NBA Cup championship, and the franchise’s first NBA title in five decades. Brunson became Finals MVP, while Towns delivered consistently on the biggest stage.

Five years after the extension, the anniversary is bittersweet. Randle never won the big prize in New York, but our appreciation for his contribution has grown in retrospect. He joined a dysfunctional franchise, restored respectability and expectations, embodied its culture of hard work, and ultimately became a valuable enough asset to help acquire the third-best center in the league (according to . . . any guesses whom they put ahead of KAT?).

On the timeline from the crappy years to the championship, Randle’s 2021 extension stands as a pivotal moment. The line extends from there through Brunson’s arrival, the Towns trade, and the hanging of the banner (coming soon!). Randle is back in New York these days, about to start a season with the Brooklyn Nets. If you see him around the city, give him a nod and show some respect. The championship we are celebrating now might not have happened without him.
